title: Logged out, and lost your place?

titles: Logged Out and Lost Your Place? The Two Kinds of Session
Why Login Sends You to the Home Page (and the Fix)
publish.description: Your progress was saved, but after logging in again you land on the home page. The word session hides two things: who you are, which should expire, and where you were, which should not.
extra: 🎬 The full video (from one laptop to a million students: local storage, progress on the server, 20k writes per second and two devices that disagree) is on the channel.
Return-to-page after login must accept only paths on your own site (OWASP: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards).
publish.comment: Have you ever lost your place like this? In which app?

scenes.heading: Logged out, and *lost your place*?
scenes.narration: You step away from a lesson for two hours. When you come back, you log in again, and land on the home page. Your progress was saved. So why did you lose your place?

scenes.title: Two kinds of session
scenes.narration: The word session hides two things. Who you are: the login. Like a hotel key card, it expires on purpose, for security. And where you were: the lesson, the second, the quiz. Like your stored luggage, it should not.

scenes.title: What went wrong
scenes.narration: Here, the login expired after two hours, and the progress was safe in its table. But the login page sends everyone home. It forgot where you were going. Making the login last longer only hides it.

scenes.title: The fix
scenes.narration: The fix: before login, keep the page they asked for. After login, send them back there, and the progress picks up at the same second. Only accept paths on your own site, or attackers can use your login page to send people anywhere.

scenes.title: Keep them apart
scenes.narration: Keep the two sessions apart: the login expires, the progress stays. And after login, send them back, to your own site only. Have you ever lost your place like this? The full video is on the channel.

notes: The auth session (a cookie or token) should expire for security; the work state should not. Mixing them, for example keeping progress in the server's session memory, makes it vanish on expiry, on a restart and across server copies.
Two hours idle is our example; OWASP's session management guidance suggests shorter idle timeouts for many apps, and that's fine: the progress lives elsewhere.

Return-to-page: save the requested path before redirecting to login (a query parameter or a short-lived cookie), and after login accept only relative paths on your own site. OWASP: unvalidated redirects let attackers send users to a phishing page with your domain in the link.
The progress itself is a row per student and course on the server (lesson, second, quiz answers, saved_at), so any device can pick up where you left off.
"Own site only" in practice: accept only paths that start with a single "/" and reject "//" and "/\", because protocol-relative URLs pass naive checks.
A save that arrives after the login expired gets a 401; the client keeps it locally and retries after the user logs in again.
